newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: GDP data takes heat off Australian debt rally.
newsitem.headline: GDP data takes heat off Australian debt rally.

text.p: *Australian debt futures slipped back from their early perkier levels after first quarter GDP came in much in line with expectations and cast some doubts over further policy easings.
*RBA keeps rates unchanged after Tuesday's board meeting.
Australian debt futures slipped back from their early perkier levels after first quarter GDP came in much in line with expectations and cast some doubts over further policy easings.

"It is very hard to build a case from these numbers why you need a another rate cut to drive domestic demand stronger," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia. "It means the bond markets here are a wee bit overvalued."
March quarter GDP rose 0.9 percent, taking the annual rate to to 2.4 percent and after a revised 0.4 percent growth in the December quarter.
Treasurer Peter Costello told reporters the data suggested the economy was poised to accelerate and saw a positive June quarter for inventories after their recent run-down.

The market had firmed strongly in pre-opening trading, taking three-year bond yields to around 6.10 percent and to their lowest level in 3-1/4 years, on the off chance the Reserve Bank this morning would ease rates again after Tuesday's policy making board meeting.
In the event, the central bank made no announcement and short bond yields subsequently firmed up to around 6.20 percent.
Bill futures also eased back from their highs, but the September contract was still trading below the official 5.5 percent cash rate by some 12 basis points.

Inflation data included in the GDP remained subdued with the GDP-E deflator rising 0.3 percent for 1.6 percent for the year. "The price deflators are very favourable ... there is not a lot of inflation coming through the national accounts," said Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas.
"I don't think we need another reactive interest rate cut. The Reserve Bank has already reacted to the slowdown and to the low inflation rate," he added.

The local market's pullback saw it underperform against the dollar bloc, apart from the long end of the Canadian curve in the aftermath of Tuesday's Canadian election result. The Liberals were returned to power as expected, albeit with a smaller majority.
